title: Static electricity — why you get zapped touching a door handle
examTip: Static electricity questions almost always ask about electron transfer. Never say protons move. Say which object gains or loses electrons, and what charge each ends up with.
introTips: Think of a time you got a static shock. That tiny spark is the same physics as a lightning bolt, just on a very different scale.
Before reading, try this. In one sentence, explain why rubbing a balloon on your hair makes it stick to a wall.
Focus on which way the electrons move. Which object gains them, which loses them, and what charge results?
intro: You walk across a carpet, touch a door handle and get a small shock. That is caused by the same basic physics as a lightning strike. In both cases, charge builds up on an insulating surface until it suddenly discharges. Static electricity explains natural things like lightning. It also explains how inkjet printers place tiny ink droplets exactly. It explains how factory paint sprayers coat car bodies evenly. And it explains why fuel tanker lorries must be earthed before filling up. A static spark near petrol vapour could be a disaster.

keyPoints.heading: Charging by friction
keyPoints.content: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one surface to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. Key rule: only electrons transfer. Protons are fixed inside atomic nuclei and cannot be moved by friction. Charge is conserved: the amount of negative charge gained equals the positive charge lost. Examples: - a polythene rod rubbed with a cloth gains electrons from the cloth. The polythene becomes negative, and the cloth becomes positive - an acetate rod rubbed with a cloth loses electrons to the cloth. The acetate becomes positive, and the cloth becomes negative Static electricity only builds up on insulators. Conductors let charge flow away. This is why a metal door handle discharges you at once. The charge flows through the conductor. But a polythene rod stays charged.
writeBullets: Friction transfers electrons, never protons. Protons are fixed in the nucleus
Object gaining electrons → negatively charged
Object losing electrons → positively charged
Charge is conserved: charge gained = charge lost (equal and opposite)
Polythene + cloth: polythene gains electrons → negative. Cloth → positive
Acetate + cloth: acetate loses electrons → positive. Cloth → negative

keyTerms.def: The transfer of electrons between two insulating surfaces when rubbed together, causing one to become positive and the other negative.
The total charge before and after friction is the same — charge gained by one object equals charge lost by the other.
A material that does not allow charge to flow through it easily; static charge can build up on insulators.

keyPoints.memTip: Electrons are the movers. Think of them as passengers getting off one bus and onto another. The bus that loses passengers (electrons) goes positive. The one that gains them goes negative.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The single most common mistake in static electricity questions is writing 'protons are transferred'. It must be electrons. Repeat this rule until it is automatic.

keyPoints.heading: Like and unlike charges
keyPoints.content: Unlike (opposite) charges attract each other. Like (same) charges repel each other. You can show this simply. Hang two negatively charged polythene rods near each other on threads. They swing apart (repel). Bring a negatively charged rod near a positively charged acetate rod. They swing towards each other (attract). The force between charges gets weaker as the distance between them grows. Everyday examples of static attraction and repulsion: - clothes clinging after a tumble dryer: different fabrics pick up opposite charges and attract - hair standing on end after pulling off a jumper: the hair strands all gain the same charge. They repel each other - dust sticking to screens: the screen becomes charged and attracts neutral dust particles Lightning: charge builds up in storm clouds. Ice crystals and water droplets collide and transfer charge. This makes the base of the cloud negatively charged. When enough charge builds up, a huge spark jumps between the cloud and the ground. That is a lightning bolt.
writeBullets: Unlike charges attract. Like charges repel
The force between charges gets weaker as the distance grows
Two charged rods with the same sign: repel (swing apart on threads)
Two charged rods with opposite signs: attract (swing together)
Lightning: charge builds in clouds from friction between ice crystals and water droplets. It discharges to the ground
Hair standing on end: the strands all have the same charge → they repel each other

keyTerms.def: The force pulling opposite charges together; unlike charges attract.
The force pushing like charges apart; same charges repel.
A massive electrostatic discharge caused by charge build-up in storm clouds; occurs when potential difference becomes large enough to ionise the air.

keyPoints.memTip: Like charges: same meets same and they push each other away (repel). Opposite charges: different attracts different. They want to cancel each other out.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say 'positive attracts positive'. LIKE charges repel and UNLIKE charges attract. Getting this backwards costs marks on every static question.

keyPoints.heading: Electric fields
keyPoints.content: A charged object creates an electric field in the space around it. Any other charged object placed in this field feels a force. The objects do not need to touch. An electric field is shown by field lines. These show the direction of the force on a small positive test charge. - Around an isolated positive charge, field lines point outward. A positive charge would be pushed away. - Around an isolated negative charge, field lines point inward. A positive test charge would be pulled in. - Between two parallel plates with opposite charges, the field is uniform. The field lines are parallel, equally spaced and at right angles to the plates. A stronger electric field is shown by closer (more dense) field lines. The field gets weaker with distance from a charged object, like a gravitational field. Electrostatic forces act at a distance. This is why a charged rod held near small bits of paper can attract them without touching.
writeBullets: Charged objects create an electric field in the space around them. No contact is needed
Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive test charge
Positive charge: field lines radiate outward
Negative charge: field lines radiate inward
Uniform field between parallel plates: parallel, equally spaced lines at right angles to the plates
Closer field lines → stronger electric field

keyTerms.def: A region of space around a charged object where another charge experiences a force.
Lines drawn to represent an electric field; show the direction of force on a positive test charge. Closer lines = stronger field.
A field of constant strength and direction, represented by parallel, equally spaced field lines. Found between two parallel plates with opposite charges.

keyPoints.memTip: Field lines are like arrows showing where a positive charge would go. From a positive source, the arrows flee outward.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A common slip is drawing field lines between parallel plates from the negative plate to the positive plate. Field lines go FROM positive TO negative. That is the way a positive charge moves.

keyPoints.heading: Dangers and uses of static electricity
keyPoints.content: Dangers: static sparks carry enough energy to ignite flammable vapours. - Fuel tanker lorries are connected to the ground by an earthing wire before the fuel hose is attached. Charge built up on the journey can then discharge safely, instead of sparking near fuel vapour. - Aircraft build up static charge in flight, from friction with the air. Bonding cables connect the aircraft and the fuelling vehicle. They drain the charge before refuelling starts. Even a small spark near fuel vapour can cause an explosion. Uses of static electricity: - Inkjet printers: ink droplets are given a charge. Electric field plates deflect the charged droplets so they hit exact spots on the paper. This builds up text and images. - Photocopiers (laser printers): a drum is charged. Laser light removes charge from areas that should stay white. Charged toner powder sticks only to the charged areas. Heat then fuses it onto the paper. - Electrostatic precipitators: these are used in factory chimneys. Charged plates attract soot and dust from the smoke. They remove up to 99% of particles before the gases reach the air. - Electrostatic paint spraying: paint droplets are all given the same charge. They repel each other, so they spread out evenly. The car body is earthed (opposite charge), so it attracts all the droplets. This gives better coverage, less waste and an even coat on complex shapes.
writeBullets: Static spark danger: sparks can ignite flammable vapours. Fuel lorries are earthed before refuelling
Aircraft bonding cables: drain static charge before fuelling starts
Inkjet printer: an electric field deflects charged ink droplets onto the paper
Photocopier: a charged drum attracts toner to the right areas. Heat fuses the toner to the paper
Electrostatic precipitator: charged plates attract soot and dust from chimney smoke
Paint spraying: charged droplets repel each other (even spread). The earthed car body attracts them

keyTerms.def: Connecting a charged object to the ground with a conductor so charge drains away safely, preventing sparks.
A device in factory chimneys that uses charged plates to attract and remove smoke particles from gases before they are released into the atmosphere.
Uses electrostatically charged ink droplets deflected by electric field plates to build up images on paper.
A conducting wire connecting an aircraft to refuelling equipment to safely discharge static build-up before fuelling.

keyPoints.memTip: For paint spraying: the same charge on the droplets = they spread out. The opposite charge on the car = they are attracted.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exam questions on uses of static often ask you to explain in terms of charge, not just describe. Say 'the charged droplets repel each other and are attracted to the earthed surface'.

tables.title: Charging by friction — summary
rows: Electrons transfer FROM cloth TO polythene
Electrons transfer FROM acetate TO cloth
Electrons transfer from hair to balloon
Positive (why hair stands up — strands repel)

0.question: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. What has happened to make the rod negatively charged?
options: Electrons have transferred from the cloth to the polythene rod
Protons have transferred from the polythene to the cloth
Electrons have transferred from the polythene to the cloth
The cloth has given the rod extra neutrons
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right. Electrons move from the cloth onto the polythene. The rod gains electrons and becomes negative. The cloth loses electrons and becomes positive.
0.wrongFeedback: Only electrons transfer. Protons and neutrons cannot be moved by friction. The polythene becomes negative because it GAINS electrons from the cloth, not because it loses anything.

1.question: Two polythene rods are both negatively charged and hung near each other. What will happen?
options: They will repel each other (move apart)
They will attract each other (move together)
One will become positive and attract the other
1.correctFeedback: Correct. Like charges repel. Both rods are negative, so they push each other away.
1.wrongFeedback: Remember: like charges REPEL. Both rods are negative (same charge), so they push each other away. Attraction only happens between opposite charges.

2.question: Why must fuel tanker lorries be earthed before the fuel hose is connected?
options: Charge built up on the journey could discharge as a spark and ignite fuel vapour. Earthing drains the charge safely
Earthing increases the pressure in the fuel hose
Earthing makes the lorry a better conductor of electricity
It is a legal requirement with no scientific basis
2.correctFeedback: Spot on. Charge builds up on the tanker during the journey. Earthing gives that charge a safe path to drain away. This stops a spark that could ignite petrol vapour.
2.wrongFeedback: The reason is all about static safety. Charge built up on the journey could discharge as a spark when the metal hose is connected. Near fuel vapour, even a small spark can cause an explosion. Earthing drains the charge to the ground first.

3.question: In electrostatic paint spraying, why are the paint droplets given the same charge as each other?
options: So they repel each other and spread out evenly, giving a more even coat
So they are attracted to each other and clump together on the surface
To make them fall faster due to gravity
To neutralise the charge on the car body
3.correctFeedback: Perfect. Like charges repel. So droplets with the same charge spread apart instead of clumping. The earthed car body also attracts them. The result is an even, efficient coat.
3.wrongFeedback: Think about like charges: they REPEL. If all the droplets carry the same charge, they push each other apart. This spreads them out evenly across the surface. The car body (earthed, opposite charge) then attracts them all.

commonMistakes: Writing that protons transfer during friction charging. Only electrons can move. Protons are locked inside the atomic nucleus and cannot be moved by rubbing.
Saying 'like charges attract'. This is the opposite of the rule. Like charges REPEL. Unlike (opposite) charges ATTRACT.
Drawing electric field lines around a negative charge pointing outward. Field lines always point inward towards a negative charge. That is the way a positive test charge would move.
Describing earthing as 'removing the electricity'. Instead, explain that charge drains through the conducting earth wire to the ground. This neutralises the object.
Mixing up 'charged' with 'has more protons'. Charge comes from gaining or losing electrons. It does not come from changing the number of protons.
examTips: When asked to explain charging by friction, always say three things. (1) What transfers: electrons. (2) Which way they move: from ___ to ___. (3) What charge each object ends up with. Three steps, three marks.

For electric field questions, remember: field lines show the direction of the force on a POSITIVE test charge. Around positive = outward. Around negative = inward. Between plates = parallel lines from the + plate to the − plate.

Questions on uses of static often ask you to explain in terms of charge. Describe the charge on each part and the force between them. Don't just say what happens. Explain why, using the words 'attracted' or 'repelled'.
